q: A patient has had most of the colon surgically removed because of disease. Which change in digestive function is most expected after the surgery?
o: Poorer uptake of vitamin B12 with intrinsic factor
Slower final breakdown of peptides by colon enzymes
Poorer absorption of glucose and amino acids
Looser stools from reduced water absorption
w: The large intestine's main job is absorbing water and electrolytes and forming feces. Removing most of the colon leaves less surface to reclaim water, so stools become looser.

n.0: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed in the ileum of the small intestine, which is not part of the colon.
n.1: The large intestine has no digestive enzymes of its own; brush-border peptidases of the small intestine finish protein digestion.
n.2: Glucose and amino acids are absorbed through the villi of the small intestine; the colon has no villi and absorbs mainly water and electrolytes.

q: A patient's terminal ileum is removed because of disease, but the duodenum and jejunum are left in place. Absorption of which nutrient is most at risk after this surgery?
o: Glucose
Vitamin B12
Vitamin K
Dietary iron
w: Vitamin B12, bound to intrinsic factor from the stomach, is absorbed in the ileum. Removing the ileum therefore threatens B12 absorption even though the rest of the small intestine remains.

n.0: Glucose is absorbed mainly in the jejunum, which is still present.
n.2: Vitamin K is fat-soluble and is supplied partly by bacteria in the large intestine, which is untouched; uptake of B12 with intrinsic factor is the ileum's specific job.
n.3: Intrinsic factor and the ileum are linked to vitamin B12, not iron; confusing them is a classic trap.

q: When the stomach is empty, its inner lining forms large folds that flatten out as a meal arrives. What are these folds called, and what is their main role?
o: Rugae, which allow the stomach to expand with food
Microvilli, which hold brush-border digestive enzymes
Circular folds, which slow chyme to aid absorption
Villi, which add surface area for absorbing nutrients
w: Rugae are the folds of the stomach lining. They flatten as the stomach fills, letting it stretch to hold a meal.

n.1: Microvilli form the brush border of small intestine cells, not folds of the stomach lining.
n.2: Circular folds belong to the small intestine wall and do not flatten when the stomach fills.
n.3: Villi are finger-like projections of the small intestine, not stomach folds.

q: Which structure controls the passage of material from the last segment of the small intestine into the large intestine?
o: Pyloric sphincter
Ileocecal valve
Lower esophageal sphincter
Hepatopancreatic sphincter
w: The ileum ends at the ileocecal valve, which opens into the cecum, the first part of the large intestine.

n.0: The pyloric sphincter controls emptying of the stomach into the duodenum.
n.2: The lower esophageal sphincter sits between the esophagus and stomach and limits reflux.
n.3: The hepatopancreatic sphincter (of Oddi) controls bile and pancreatic juice entering the duodenum.

q: Digestion includes both mechanical and chemical processes. Which pairing of a digestive process with its type of digestion is correct?
o: Segmentation mixing chyme in the small intestine: mechanical
Lactase splitting lactose at the brush border: mechanical
Churning of food by the stomach's muscle layers: chemical
Salivary amylase breaking starch into maltose: mechanical
w: Mechanical digestion physically breaks up and mixes food: chewing, stomach churning and segmentation in the small intestine. Enzymes breaking chemical bonds is chemical digestion.

n.1: Lactase is an enzyme that hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose, so this is chemical digestion.
n.2: Churning physically breaks up and mixes food without breaking chemical bonds, so it is mechanical digestion.
n.3: Salivary amylase is an enzyme that breaks chemical bonds in starch, so this is chemical digestion.

q: A clinic handout reviews the jobs of the digestive organs that food does not pass through. Which of the following functions is carried out by the liver?
o: Converting ammonia into urea
Storing and concentrating bile
Producing insulin and glucagon
Secreting trypsinogen into the duodenum
w: The liver converts toxic ammonia from protein breakdown into urea, which the kidneys then excrete. It also makes bile, stores glycogen, detoxifies drugs and alcohol, and makes plasma proteins.

n.1: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile; the liver makes it.
n.2: Insulin and glucagon come from the islets of the pancreas, its endocrine part.
n.3: Trypsinogen is made by the acinar cells of the exocrine pancreas.

q: A student chews a plain cracker for a full minute without swallowing and notices that it begins to taste slightly sweet. Which enzyme best explains this?
o: Salivary amylase
Pancreatic amylase
Lingual lipase
Brush-border maltase
w: Salivary amylase starts the chemical digestion of starch in the mouth, breaking it into smaller sugars that taste sweet.

n.1: Pancreatic amylase digests starch in the duodenum, not in the mouth.
n.2: Lingual lipase is in saliva, but it acts on fats, not starch.
n.3: Maltase splits maltose into glucose, but it sits on the brush border of the small intestine, not in the mouth.

q: Which pairing of an accessory digestive organ with something it secretes into the digestive tract is correct?
o: Salivary glands: pepsinogen
Gallbladder: bile that it produces
Pancreas: bicarbonate and lipase
Liver: trypsin and chymotrypsin
w: The exocrine pancreas releases pancreatic juice containing bicarbonate (to neutralize acid chyme) and enzymes such as lipase, amylase, trypsinogen and nucleases.

n.0: Pepsinogen is made by chief cells in the stomach; saliva contains amylase and lingual lipase.
n.1: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile, but the liver produces it.
n.3: Trypsin and chymotrypsin are pancreatic enzymes; the liver makes bile, not digestive enzymes.

q: A patient asks how she will digest fat after her gallbladder is removed. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Her pancreas will take over storing bile
Her stomach digests most fat, so bile is less needed
Her liver still makes bile that reaches the duodenum
Her small intestine will make the lipase it once supplied
w: The liver, not the gallbladder, makes bile. Without a gallbladder, bile from the liver still drains into the duodenum to emulsify fat; it is simply not stored and concentrated between meals.

n.0: The pancreas makes pancreatic juice and does not store bile.
n.1: Most fat digestion happens in the small intestine, not the stomach.
n.3: The gallbladder never supplied lipase; lipase comes from the pancreas.

q: Bile salts released into the duodenum are essential for normal fat digestion. Which statement correctly describes how bile salts act on dietary fat?
o: They convert inactive pepsinogen into pepsin
They carry fats into villus blood capillaries
They break large fat droplets into smaller ones
They hydrolyze triglycerides into fatty acids
w: Bile is not an enzyme. Bile salts emulsify fat, breaking large droplets into many small ones so pancreatic lipase has more surface to act on.

n.0: Pepsinogen is activated by hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
n.1: Digested fats are absorbed into lacteals (lymph), not blood capillaries.
n.3: Splitting fats into fatty acids is chemical digestion by pancreatic lipase, not by bile.

q: Shortly after a meal high in fat, cells of the duodenum release a hormone that makes the gallbladder contract. Which hormone is this, and what other effect does it have?
o: Secretin; it also triggers pancreatic bicarbonate release
Glucagon; it also triggers glycogen breakdown
Gastrin; it also triggers gastric acid secretion
Cholecystokinin; it also triggers pancreatic enzyme release
w: Cholecystokinin (CCK) from the duodenum makes the gallbladder contract to release bile and stimulates the pancreas to release its digestive enzymes.

n.0: Secretin does trigger bicarbonate release from the pancreas, but it is not the hormone that contracts the gallbladder.
n.1: Glucagon is a pancreatic islet hormone that raises blood glucose; it is not a duodenal hormone.
n.2: Gastrin comes from the stomach and stimulates acid secretion; it does not contract the gallbladder.

q: When acidic chyme enters the duodenum, a hormone is released that signals the pancreas to secrete a fluid rich in bicarbonate. Which hormone sends this signal?
o: Secretin
Glucagon
Cholecystokinin
Gastrin
w: Secretin from the duodenum causes the pancreas to release bicarbonate, which neutralizes acid chyme arriving from the stomach.

n.1: Glucagon is an islet hormone that raises blood glucose and does not control bicarbonate.
n.2: Cholecystokinin mainly triggers pancreatic enzyme release and gallbladder contraction.
n.3: Gastrin is a stomach hormone that increases acid secretion, the opposite of neutralizing it.

q: Blood leaving the capillaries of the small intestine carries newly absorbed sugars and amino acids. To which organ does this blood travel first for processing, and by which vessel?
o: The liver, by the hepatic artery
The heart, by the inferior vena cava
The liver, by the hepatic portal vein
The liver, by the hepatic veins
w: Nutrient-rich blood from the intestines drains into the hepatic portal vein, which delivers it to the liver for processing before it reaches the general circulation.

n.0: The hepatic artery brings oxygen-rich blood from the aorta to the liver, not nutrient-rich blood from the intestines.
n.1: Blood from the intestines reaches the inferior vena cava only after it has passed through the liver.
n.3: The hepatic veins drain blood out of the liver into the inferior vena cava; they do not bring intestinal blood to it.

q: A patient with severe liver failure has a low blood albumin level and bleeds easily from minor cuts. Which loss of liver function best explains both findings?
o: Reduced synthesis of plasma proteins
Reduced storage of glycogen
Reduced conversion of ammonia to urea
Reduced production of bile salts
w: The liver makes plasma proteins, including albumin and clotting factors such as fibrinogen and prothrombin. Losing this function explains both the low albumin and the easy bleeding.

n.1: Glycogen storage affects blood glucose control, not albumin or clotting.
n.2: Failing urea production raises blood ammonia; it does not lower albumin or impair clotting.
n.3: Less bile could reduce fat-soluble vitamin absorption, but it would not explain the low albumin.

q: The pancreas has an exocrine part and an endocrine part. Which of these products is released through ducts into the duodenum rather than into the blood?
o: Somatostatin made by delta cells
Insulin made by beta cells
Glucagon made by alpha cells
Trypsinogen made by acinar cells
w: Acinar cells of the exocrine pancreas make pancreatic juice, including trypsinogen, which travels through ducts to the duodenum. Islet hormones enter the blood.

n.0: Somatostatin is an islet hormone that acts on other islet cells; it is not part of pancreatic juice.
n.1: Insulin is an endocrine hormone from the islets and enters the blood, not a duct.
n.2: Glucagon is an islet hormone secreted into the blood to raise blood glucose.

q: A gallstone blocks the bile duct before it joins the pancreatic duct, so bile cannot reach the duodenum. Which digestive process in the small intestine is most directly impaired?
o: Splitting of maltose by brush-border maltase
Emulsification of dietary fat
Breakdown of protein by trypsin
Absorption of glucose into villus capillaries
w: Bile salts emulsify fat. If bile cannot reach the duodenum, fat stays in large droplets, so fat digestion by lipase and its absorption suffer.

n.0: Maltase sits on the microvilli of the small intestine and splits maltose without any help from bile.
n.2: Trypsin comes from the pancreas; the block is above the pancreatic duct, so pancreatic juice still flows.
n.3: Glucose is absorbed into the blood capillaries of the villi, a process that does not depend on bile.

q: A patient eats a lunch of grilled chicken, which is mostly protein. In which organ does chemical digestion of this protein begin, and which enzyme starts it?
o: The mouth, by salivary amylase
The duodenum, by trypsin
The mouth, by lingual lipase
The stomach, by pepsin
w: Protein digestion begins in the stomach, where pepsin (activated from pepsinogen by hydrochloric acid) breaks proteins into shorter peptides. Carbohydrate digestion is the one that begins in the mouth.

n.0: Salivary amylase digests starch, not protein; protein digestion does not begin in the mouth.
n.1: Trypsin continues protein digestion in the small intestine after pepsin has started it in the stomach.
n.2: Lingual lipase acts on fats, and protein digestion does not begin in the mouth.

q: After pancreatic lipase splits dietary fats into fatty acids and monoglycerides, intestinal cells repackage them for absorption. Into which vessels do these fats first pass, and in what form?
o: Villus blood capillaries, as free fatty acids
Lacteals in the villi, as monosaccharides
The hepatic portal vein, as triglycerides
Lacteals in the villi, as chylomicrons
w: Absorptive cells package digested fats into chylomicrons, which are too large for blood capillaries and enter the lacteals, the lymphatic capillaries of the villi.

n.0: Sugars and amino acids enter blood capillaries; fats enter the lymph through lacteals.
n.1: Lacteals are the right vessels, but monosaccharides are sugars and are absorbed into blood capillaries.
n.2: The hepatic portal vein carries absorbed sugars and amino acids to the liver, not chylomicrons.

q: Brush-border enzymes complete the chemical digestion of carbohydrates in the small intestine. Which set lists the end products that are absorbed into the blood?
o: Starch, glycogen and glucose
Glucose, fructose and galactose
Glycerol, fatty acids and glucose
Maltose, sucrose and lactose
w: Carbohydrates are absorbed only as monosaccharides: glucose, fructose and galactose. Maltase, sucrase and lactase split the disaccharides to produce them.

n.0: Starch and glycogen are polysaccharides, far too large to be absorbed.
n.2: Glycerol and fatty acids come from fat digestion, not carbohydrate digestion.
n.3: Maltose, sucrose and lactose are disaccharides that brush-border enzymes still have to split before absorption.

q: A person who makes too little lactase has cramping and bloating after drinking milk. Where is lactase normally produced and active?
o: In gastric juice secreted by chief cells
On the brush border of the small intestine
In saliva secreted by the parotid glands
In pancreatic juice from the acinar cells
w: Lactase is a brush-border enzyme on the microvilli of the small intestine, along with maltase, sucrase and peptidases. It splits lactose into glucose and galactose.

n.0: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen for protein digestion.
n.2: Saliva contains salivary amylase and lingual lipase, not lactase.
n.3: Pancreatic juice contains amylase, lipase, proteases and nucleases, but lactase is a brush-border enzyme.

q: Parietal cells in the stomach lining secrete hydrochloric acid, which keeps gastric pH very low. Which of the following is a role of this acid?
o: Binding vitamin B12 for uptake in the ileum
Emulsifying fat droplets so lipase can act
Activating pancreatic trypsinogen into trypsin
Converting pepsinogen into active pepsin
w: Hydrochloric acid activates pepsinogen into pepsin, which begins protein digestion, and it kills many swallowed microbes.

n.0: Binding vitamin B12 is the role of intrinsic factor, the other product of parietal cells, not the acid.
n.1: Emulsifying fat is the job of bile salts in the duodenum, not stomach acid.
n.2: Trypsinogen is activated in the duodenum by the brush-border enzyme enteropeptidase (and then by trypsin itself), not by stomach acid.

q: An autoimmune disease destroys a patient's gastric parietal cells. Which pair of problems would be expected as a result?
o: Poor fat emulsification and poor vitamin K production
Poor trypsin activation and poor amino acid absorption
Poor pepsin activation and poor vitamin B12 absorption
Poor bicarbonate release and poor glucose absorption
w: Parietal cells make hydrochloric acid, which activates pepsin, and intrinsic factor, which is needed to absorb vitamin B12 in the ileum. Losing them impairs both.

n.0: Fat emulsification depends on bile from the liver, and vitamin K is made by colon bacteria.
n.1: Trypsin is activated in the small intestine and comes from the pancreas; amino acid absorption continues there.
n.3: Bicarbonate comes from the pancreas, and glucose is absorbed in the small intestine.

q: Which enzyme is correctly matched with both the site where it acts and the nutrient it digests?
o: Pancreatic lipase: small intestine; starch
Salivary amylase: small intestine; starch
Pepsin: stomach; proteins
Trypsin: stomach; proteins
w: Pepsin acts in the stomach on proteins. Each other option gets either the site or the nutrient wrong.

n.0: Pancreatic lipase does act in the small intestine, but it digests fats, not starch.
n.1: Salivary amylase digests starch, but it acts in the mouth; pancreatic amylase digests starch in the small intestine.
n.3: Trypsin digests proteins, but it acts in the small intestine, where pancreatic juice enters, not in the stomach.

q: A meal contains bread, lean turkey and butter. When the resulting chyme first enters the duodenum, which statement about the chemical digestion of this meal is accurate?
o: Protein digestion has begun; starch and fat digestion have not
Starch and protein digestion have begun; most fat digestion has not
Starch digestion has begun; protein and fat digestion have not
Fat and protein digestion have begun; starch digestion has not
w: Step 1: starch digestion begins in the mouth with salivary amylase. Step 2: protein digestion begins in the stomach with pepsin. Fat digestion is mostly in the small intestine, after bile and pancreatic lipase act (lingual lipase does very little), so most fat digestion has not yet occurred.

n.0: Starch digestion began in the mouth with salivary amylase, before the stomach.
n.2: Protein digestion has already begun in the stomach by the time chyme reaches the duodenum.
n.3: Most fat digestion waits for bile and pancreatic lipase in the small intestine, while starch digestion began in the mouth.

q: A patient drinks tea sweetened with table sugar (sucrose). Which brush-border enzyme digests the sucrose, and which monosaccharides are then absorbed?
o: Sucrase; glucose and galactose
Maltase; glucose and fructose
Lactase; glucose and galactose
Sucrase; glucose and fructose
w: Sucrase on the microvilli of the small intestine splits sucrose into glucose and fructose, which enter the villus blood capillaries. Lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose, and maltase splits maltose into two glucose molecules.

n.0: Sucrase is the right enzyme, but glucose plus galactose are the products of lactose, not sucrose.
n.1: Maltase splits maltose into two glucose molecules; it does not act on sucrose.
n.2: Lactase splits lactose (milk sugar) into glucose and galactose; sucrose is digested by sucrase.

q: Which vitamin is fat-soluble and is also made in part by bacteria living in the large intestine?
o: Vitamin D
Vitamin K
Vitamin C
Vitamin B12
w: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and are absorbed with dietary fat. Bacteria in the large intestine make vitamin K (and some B vitamins), so vitamin K meets both conditions.

n.0: Vitamin D is fat-soluble, but its precursor is made in the skin with UVB light, not by gut bacteria.
n.2: Vitamin C is water-soluble and comes from the diet; intestinal bacteria do not supply it.
n.3: Colon bacteria do make some B vitamins, but vitamin B12 is water-soluble, not fat-soluble.

q: A patient's imaging report describes a small stone lodged partway along the tube that carries urine from the left kidney to the urinary bladder. In which structure is the stone located?
o: Ureter
Urethra
Collecting duct
Renal pelvis
w: Each ureter carries urine from a kidney to the urinary bladder by peristalsis. The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the outside.

n.1: The urethra drains the bladder to the outside; mixing up ureter and urethra is a classic trap.
n.2: Collecting ducts lie inside the kidney medulla and carry urine toward the calyces.
n.3: The renal pelvis is the funnel inside the kidney that collects urine and leads into the ureter.

q: Filtrate leaving the ascending limb of the nephron loop flows next into which part of the nephron?
o: Descending limb of the loop
Distal convoluted tubule
Proximal convoluted tubule
Collecting duct
w: Filtrate path: glomerular capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, descending limb, ascending limb of the nephron loop, distal convoluted tubule, then the collecting duct.

n.0: The descending limb comes before the ascending limb, so the filtrate has already passed through it.
n.2: The proximal convoluted tubule comes before the nephron loop, directly after the glomerular capsule.
n.3: The collecting duct receives filtrate from the distal convoluted tubule, one step later than the segment asked for.

q: Blood enters each glomerulus through one arteriole and leaves through another. Which vessel delivers blood into the glomerulus?
o: Efferent arteriole
Peritubular capillary
Afferent arteriole
Vasa recta
w: The afferent arteriole carries blood into the glomerulus; the efferent arteriole carries it out to the peritubular capillaries. (Afferent = arrives; efferent = exits.)

n.0: The efferent arteriole carries blood out of the glomerulus, not into it.
n.1: Peritubular capillaries receive blood from the efferent arteriole after it leaves the glomerulus.
n.3: The vasa recta are capillaries that branch from efferent arterioles around the nephron loops; they receive blood after the glomerulus.

q: The renal corpuscle is the part of the nephron where blood is first filtered. Which two structures together make up the renal corpuscle?
o: Glomerulus and proximal convoluted tubule
Glomerular capsule and nephron loop
Afferent and efferent arterioles
Glomerulus and glomerular capsule
w: The renal corpuscle is the glomerulus (capillary tuft) surrounded by the glomerular (Bowman's) capsule. Filtration happens there, not in the tubule.

n.0: The proximal convoluted tubule follows the capsule; it is part of the renal tubule, not the corpuscle.
n.1: The nephron loop (loop of Henle) is part of the tubule and lies mainly in the medulla.
n.2: These arterioles supply and drain the glomerulus but are not the corpuscle itself.

q: The wall of the urinary bladder must stretch a great deal as it fills with urine. Which tissue lines the bladder and allows this stretching?
o: Simple columnar epithelium
Simple squamous epithelium
Stratified squamous epithelium
Transitional epithelium
w: The bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), whose cells change shape from rounded to flattened as the bladder fills.

n.0: Simple columnar epithelium lines much of the digestive tract and is built for secretion and absorption.
n.1: Simple squamous epithelium is a thin layer built for diffusion and filtration, not for stretching.
n.2: Stratified squamous epithelium resists abrasion, as in the skin and esophagus, but does not stretch like urothelium.

q: A surgeon reviews the location of the kidneys before a kidney procedure. Which statement about kidney position is correct?
o: They lie behind the peritoneum, the right slightly lower
They lie inside the peritoneal cavity, the right slightly lower
They lie inside the peritoneal cavity, the left slightly lower
They lie behind the peritoneum, the left slightly lower
w: The kidneys are retroperitoneal, at about T12 to L3. The liver sits above the right kidney, so it lies slightly lower than the left. The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys.

n.1: The right kidney is lower, but the kidneys are retroperitoneal, not inside the peritoneal cavity.
n.2: Both parts are wrong: the kidneys are retroperitoneal, and the right one sits lower because of the liver.
n.3: The kidneys are retroperitoneal, but the right kidney, not the left, sits lower because the liver lies above it.

q: Urination involves two sphincters around the urethra. Which statement correctly describes these sphincters?
o: Both are smooth muscle, and both are under involuntary control
Internal is smooth and involuntary; external is skeletal and voluntary
Both are skeletal muscle, and both are under voluntary control
Internal is skeletal and voluntary; external is smooth and involuntary
w: The internal urethral sphincter is smooth muscle under involuntary control; the external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle, so it can be voluntarily controlled.

n.0: The internal sphincter is smooth and involuntary, but the external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control.
n.2: The external sphincter is skeletal and voluntary, but the internal sphincter is smooth muscle and involuntary.
n.3: This reverses the two: the internal sphincter is the smooth, involuntary one.

q: During micturition, which structure contracts to push urine out of the urinary bladder and into the urethra?
o: Internal urethral sphincter
Detrusor muscle
Smooth muscle of the ureters
External urethral sphincter
w: The detrusor is the smooth muscle of the bladder wall. In micturition it contracts while the internal (involuntary, smooth) and external (voluntary, skeletal) urethral sphincters relax, so urine flows into the urethra.

n.0: The internal urethral sphincter relaxes during micturition so urine can leave; it holds urine in rather than expelling it.
n.2: Ureteral smooth muscle moves urine from the kidneys into the bladder by peristalsis; it does not empty the bladder.
n.3: The external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle that is voluntarily relaxed to allow urination; it does not push urine out.

q: Several structures pass through the hilum on the medial side of each kidney. Which statement correctly describes these structures and their direction of flow?
o: The renal vein enters; the renal artery and ureter exit
The renal artery enters; the renal vein and ureter exit
The renal vein and ureter enter; the renal artery exits
The renal artery and ureter enter; the renal vein exits
w: At the hilum, the renal artery brings blood in, while the renal vein carries blood out and the ureter carries urine out to the bladder.

n.0: Arteries carry blood to an organ, so the renal artery enters and the renal vein exits.
n.2: Both directions are reversed: the renal artery brings blood in, and the renal vein and ureter carry blood and urine out.
n.3: The renal artery does enter, but the ureter carries urine away from the kidney, so it exits.

q: About 99% of the filtrate formed each day is returned to the blood. Which part of the nephron reabsorbs the largest share of the filtered water and sodium?
o: Collecting duct
Ascending limb of the nephron loop
Proximal convoluted tubule
Distal convoluted tubule
w: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the most: normally all of the glucose and amino acids and about 65% of the sodium and water, plus bicarbonate.

n.0: The collecting duct fine-tunes water reabsorption under ADH, but it handles a much smaller share than the PCT.
n.1: The ascending limb pumps out sodium and chloride but is impermeable to water.
n.3: The DCT fine-tunes sodium, potassium and calcium under hormones; it is not the main site of bulk reabsorption.

q: A routine urinalysis shows a large amount of protein in a patient's urine, while the rest of the results are normal. Damage to which part of the nephron is most likely?
o: Distal convoluted tubule
Nephron loop
Glomerulus
Collecting duct
w: Large plasma proteins are normally kept out of the filtrate by the glomerular filter. Protein in the urine therefore suggests glomerular damage.

n.0: The DCT fine-tunes ions under hormonal control; filtration happens in the renal corpuscle.
n.1: The nephron loop builds the medullary concentration gradient; it is not the protein filter.
n.3: The collecting duct adjusts water reabsorption; it does not decide whether proteins enter the filtrate.

q: A fasting patient's urine test is positive for glucose. In a healthy kidney, where is filtered glucose reabsorbed, and what condition does this finding most suggest?
o: Collecting duct; diabetes mellitus
Collecting duct; diabetes insipidus
Proximal tubule; diabetes insipidus
Proximal tubule; diabetes mellitus
w: Step 1: the PCT normally reabsorbs all filtered glucose, so urine contains none. Step 2: glucose in the urine (glycosuria) means blood glucose is so high that the PCT is overwhelmed, which suggests diabetes mellitus.

n.0: Diabetes mellitus is the right condition, but glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT, not the collecting duct.
n.1: Glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT, and diabetes insipidus causes large volumes of dilute urine, not glucose in urine.
n.2: The PCT is the right site, but diabetes insipidus is an ADH problem causing dilute urine, not glucose in urine.

q: After several hours of yard work on a hot day without drinking water, a man's blood becomes more concentrated and his ADH level rises. Where does ADH act, and what is the effect on his urine?
o: Proximal tubule; urine becomes more dilute
Collecting duct; urine becomes more concentrated
Collecting duct; urine becomes more dilute
Proximal tubule; urine becomes more concentrated
w: ADH from the posterior pituitary inserts aquaporins in the collecting ducts, so more water is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced.

n.0: Both parts are wrong: ADH acts on the collecting duct and makes urine more concentrated, lowering its volume.
n.2: ADH increases water reabsorption, so urine becomes more concentrated, not more dilute.
n.3: ADH acts on the collecting duct, not the PCT; the PCT reabsorbs water mainly without hormonal control.

q: Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex acts on the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. What is its effect on the handling of sodium and potassium?
o: Water is reabsorbed while sodium is unchanged
Sodium is reabsorbed and potassium is secreted
Sodium and potassium are both reabsorbed
Potassium is reabsorbed and sodium is secreted
w: Aldosterone makes the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb sodium (water follows) and secrete potassium, raising blood volume and blood pressure.

n.0: Water reabsorption with no change in sodium describes ADH, not aldosterone.
n.2: Aldosterone increases potassium secretion into the urine, not potassium reabsorption.
n.3: This reverses aldosterone's action, a common trap: it keeps sodium and excretes potassium.

q: A drop in blood pressure triggers the release of renin, the first step in a chain that raises blood pressure again. Which statement about renin is correct?
o: It is an enzyme in the lungs that forms angiotensin II
It is an enzyme from juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney
It is a hormone secreted by the adrenal cortex
It is a hormone from the heart atria that lowers pressure
w: Renin is an enzyme released by juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney when blood pressure or sodium is low. It converts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.

n.0: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), found mostly in the lungs, forms angiotensin II; renin acts earlier.
n.2: The adrenal cortex releases aldosterone later in the pathway; renin comes from the kidney.
n.3: ANP from the atria lowers blood pressure; renin is part of the system that raises it.

q: After drinking several beers at a party, a woman produces a large volume of pale, dilute urine. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Alcohol inhibits ADH, so collecting ducts reclaim less water
Alcohol blocks glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Alcohol stimulates ADH, which increases urine output
Alcohol raises aldosterone, so more sodium is excreted
w: Alcohol inhibits ADH release. With less ADH, fewer aquaporins sit in the collecting ducts, less water is reabsorbed, and a large volume of dilute urine results.

n.1: Blocked glucose reabsorption would put glucose in the urine; that is not how alcohol increases urine volume.
n.2: ADH reduces urine output; alcohol inhibits it rather than stimulating it.
n.3: Aldosterone causes sodium reabsorption, not sodium excretion.

q: A patient receives a large volume of intravenous fluid, and the increased blood volume stretches the walls of the heart's atria. Which response helps return blood volume toward normal?
o: ADH is released, adding aquaporins to collecting ducts
Renin is released, increasing angiotensin II
ANP is released, increasing sodium and water excretion
ANP is released, increasing sodium reabsorption
w: Stretched atria release atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), which makes the kidneys lose more sodium and water, lowering blood volume and blood pressure: the opposite of RAAS.

n.0: ADH increases water reabsorption, which would raise blood volume further.
n.1: Renin and angiotensin II raise blood volume and pressure, which would worsen the overload.
n.3: ANP is the right hormone, but it increases sodium excretion; sodium reabsorption is aldosterone's effect.

q: During a panic attack, a patient breathes rapidly and deeply for several minutes. Which change in arterial blood is expected?
o: CO2 falls and pH falls: respiratory acidosis
CO2 rises and pH falls: respiratory acidosis
CO2 falls and pH rises: respiratory alkalosis
Bicarbonate falls, pH falls: metabolic acidosis
w: Hyperventilation blows off CO2. Less CO2 means less carbonic acid and fewer H⁺ ions, so blood pH rises above 7.45: respiratory alkalosis. Respiratory problems change CO2; metabolic problems change bicarbonate.

n.0: Losing CO2 removes acid from the blood, so pH rises rather than falls.
n.1: Rising CO2 with acidosis follows hypoventilation (slow, shallow breathing), the opposite of this pattern.
n.3: A primary fall in bicarbonate is metabolic acidosis, as in diabetic ketoacidosis; rapid breathing changes CO2 first.

q: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has an arterial blood pH of 7.28. Which response by the kidneys helps return the pH toward normal?
o: Secreting more H⁺ and reabsorbing more bicarbonate
Removing more CO2 to lower the carbonic acid
Retaining more H⁺ and excreting more bicarbonate
Releasing more renin to raise the blood pressure
w: Diabetic ketoacidosis is a metabolic acidosis (pH below 7.35). The kidneys, the slowest but most powerful defense, correct it by secreting H⁺ into the urine and reabsorbing and making bicarbonate, which buffers acid in the blood.

n.1: CO2 is removed by the lungs through faster, deeper breathing, not by the kidneys.
n.2: This is the reverse of the kidneys' response to acidosis: keeping H⁺ and losing bicarbonate would lower the pH further.
n.3: Renin starts the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which raises blood pressure; it does not correct blood pH.

q: Blood plasma belongs to which body fluid compartment, and which other fluid shares that compartment?
o: Extracellular fluid; interstitial fluid
Intracellular fluid; interstitial fluid
Extracellular fluid; cytosol of red cells
Intracellular fluid; cytosol of all cells
w: Body water is split into intracellular fluid (inside cells, the larger share) and extracellular fluid. Extracellular fluid is plasma plus interstitial fluid, the fluid that bathes the cells in the tissues.

n.1: Interstitial fluid lies outside cells, and so does plasma, so neither belongs to the intracellular compartment.
n.2: Plasma is extracellular, but the cytosol inside red blood cells is intracellular fluid.
n.3: Cytosol is intracellular fluid, but plasma lies outside cells and is extracellular.

q: Which pairing correctly names the main cation inside cells and the main cation in the extracellular fluid?
o: Inside K⁺; outside Cl⁻
Inside Na⁺; outside K⁺
Inside Ca²⁺; outside Na⁺
Inside K⁺; outside Na⁺
w: Potassium (K⁺) is the main cation inside cells and governs nerve and heart excitability. Sodium (Na⁺) is the main cation outside cells and controls extracellular fluid volume. Chloride (Cl⁻) is the main extracellular anion.

n.0: Potassium is right for inside cells, but chloride is an anion; the main extracellular cation is sodium.
n.1: This reverses the pair, a classic trap: sodium is mainly extracellular and potassium mainly intracellular.
n.2: Calcium is kept at very low levels inside cells; it is stored in bone and works in clotting and muscle contraction.

q: Blood pH starts to fall. Which defense acts within seconds, and which defense is the slowest but most powerful?
o: The kidneys act in seconds; the lungs are slowest
The lungs act in seconds; buffers are slowest
Buffers act in seconds; the kidneys are slowest
Buffers act in seconds; the lungs are slowest
w: Chemical buffers such as the bicarbonate-carbonic acid system bind added H⁺ almost at once. The lungs adjust CO2 within minutes. The kidneys take hours to days but are the most powerful, secreting H⁺ and reabsorbing or making bicarbonate.

n.0: The kidneys are the slowest defense, taking hours to days, not seconds.
n.1: The lungs need minutes to change CO2, and buffers are the fastest defense, not the slowest.
n.3: Buffers are the fastest, but the lungs act within minutes; the kidneys are the slowest defense.

q: Luteinizing hormone (LH) from the anterior pituitary acts on the testes. Which cells does LH stimulate, and what do those cells secrete in response?
o: Interstitial (Leydig) cells, which secrete testosterone
Interstitial (Leydig) cells, which secrete inhibin
Sustentacular (Sertoli) cells, which secrete testosterone
Sustentacular (Sertoli) cells, which secrete inhibin
w: LH stimulates the interstitial (Leydig) cells, which lie between the seminiferous tubules, to secrete testosterone. FSH is the pituitary hormone that acts on the Sertoli cells.

n.1: Leydig cells are the right target, but inhibin is secreted by Sertoli cells, not Leydig cells.
n.2: Sertoli cells are the nurse cells that support spermatogenesis; testosterone comes from the Leydig cells.
n.3: Sertoli cells do secrete inhibin, but they respond to FSH, not LH.

q: A student is labeling a diagram of the male reproductive system. Which location should she label as the site where spermatogenesis, the production of sperm, takes place?
o: Lumen of the ductus deferens
Interstitial tissue of the testis
Coiled duct of the epididymis
Seminiferous tubules of the testis
w: Sperm are produced in the seminiferous tubules of the testis, supported by Sertoli cells. They then move to the epididymis to mature and be stored.

n.0: The ductus deferens carries sperm from the epididymis toward the ejaculatory duct; it does not produce them.
n.1: The interstitial tissue between the tubules holds the Leydig cells, which make testosterone, not sperm.
n.2: The epididymis is where sperm mature and are stored after they are made, not where they are produced.

q: Semen is a mixture of sperm and fluid from several accessory glands. Which gland contributes the largest share of semen volume, and what does its fluid contain?
o: Prostate gland, which adds a milky fluid containing PSA
Seminal vesicles, which add an alkaline fluid rich in fructose
Bulbourethral glands, which add a clear lubricating mucus
Prostate gland, which adds an alkaline fluid rich in fructose
w: The seminal vesicles supply most of the semen volume: an alkaline, fructose-rich fluid (with prostaglandins) that fuels the sperm.

n.0: This describes prostate fluid correctly, but the prostate contributes less of the volume than the seminal vesicles.
n.2: The bulbourethral glands release a small amount of clear mucus before ejaculation, a minor share of semen volume.
n.3: The fructose-rich alkaline fluid comes from the seminal vesicles; prostate fluid is milky and slightly acidic.

q: To fertilize a secondary oocyte, a sperm must digest a path through the layers surrounding it. Which part of the sperm holds the enzymes that make this possible?
o: The acrosome capping the head
The mitochondria of the midpiece
The nucleus within the head
The flagellum forming the tail
w: The acrosome is a cap over the sperm head filled with enzymes that let the sperm penetrate the layers around the oocyte.

n.1: The midpiece mitochondria supply ATP for movement, not enzymes for penetrating the oocyte.
n.2: The nucleus carries the 23 chromosomes the sperm delivers; it does not hold the penetrating enzymes.
n.3: The flagellum propels the sperm; it does not digest the oocyte's outer layers.

q: After a vasectomy, a man's semen contains no sperm, yet its volume is only slightly reduced. Which explanation accounts for this?
o: Most of the fluid enters past the cut, from the seminal vesicles and prostate
Most of the fluid comes from the seminiferous tubules, which keep secreting
Most of the fluid is made in the epididymis, which lies past the cut
Most of the fluid comes from the bulbourethral glands, which drain into the ductus
w: Two steps. (1) A vasectomy cuts the ductus (vas) deferens, so sperm from the seminiferous tubules and epididymis cannot pass. (2) The seminal vesicles, which supply most of the semen volume, join the tract at the ejaculatory duct, and the prostate surrounds the urethra; both lie downstream of the cut, so their fluid still makes up most of the semen.

n.1: The seminiferous tubules produce sperm and lie upstream of the cut, so nothing from them reaches the ejaculate.
n.2: The epididymis lies before the ductus deferens, upstream of the cut, and it matures and stores sperm rather than making most of the semen fluid.
n.3: The bulbourethral glands add a small amount of mucus, and they drain into the urethra, not the ductus deferens.

q: In a man, Sertoli cells increase their secretion of inhibin as sperm production rises. Which hormonal change follows most directly from the higher inhibin level?
o: Higher GnRH secretion by the hypothalamus
Lower testosterone secretion by the Sertoli cells
Lower FSH secretion by the anterior pituitary
Lower LH secretion by the anterior pituitary
w: Inhibin from Sertoli cells is a negative-feedback signal that suppresses FSH release from the anterior pituitary, slowing spermatogenesis. Testosterone is the main feedback signal that holds LH in check.

n.0: Inhibin is an inhibitory feedback signal, so it would not raise GnRH output.
n.1: Sertoli cells do not secrete testosterone; Leydig cells do, under LH control.
n.3: LH is held in check mainly by testosterone feedback; inhibin targets FSH.

q: The testes sit in the scrotum, outside the pelvic cavity, instead of inside the abdomen. Which statement best explains why this position matters for sperm production?
o: Sperm mature inside the scrotal sac before they move into the epididymis
Spermatogenesis works best about 2 to 3 degrees Celsius below core body temperature
Spermatogenesis works best about 2 to 3 degrees Celsius above core body temperature
Leydig cells stop secreting testosterone when held at core body temperature
w: Spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules works best at about 2 to 3 degrees Celsius below core body temperature, so the scrotum holds the testes outside the body cavity.

n.0: Sperm mature in the epididymis after leaving the seminiferous tubules, not in the scrotal sac before reaching it.
n.2: The scrotum keeps the testes cooler than the body core, not warmer.
n.3: The position matters for spermatogenesis in the tubules; testosterone secretion by Leydig cells is not what the cooler setting protects.

q: A normal human sperm cell fertilizes a normal secondary oocyte. Which statement about the chromosomes carried by that sperm is correct?
o: It is haploid with 23 chromosomes, carrying either an X or a Y chromosome
It is diploid, carrying 46 chromosomes including one X and one Y
It is haploid with 23 chromosomes, and the egg's chromosome sets the child's sex
It is haploid with 23 chromosomes, each sperm carrying an X chromosome
w: Meiosis makes sperm haploid (n = 23). Each sperm carries either an X or a Y, so the sperm determines the child's sex; the egg carries an X. Fertilization restores the diploid number (2n = 46).

n.1: Gametes are haploid; 46 chromosomes is the diploid number restored at fertilization.
n.2: The egg carries an X in every case, so it is the sperm's X or Y that sets the child's sex.
n.3: It is the egg that carries an X in every case; sperm carry either an X or a Y.

q: A semen analysis shows sperm with normal heads and tails but abnormal midpieces. Which function would be most directly impaired in these sperm?
o: Releasing enzymes that digest the oocyte's outer layers
Supplying the ATP that powers movement of the tail
Storing the fructose that sperm use as an energy source
Delivering 23 chromosomes to the oocyte at fertilization
w: The midpiece is packed with mitochondria that make ATP to power the flagellum. A defective midpiece leaves the tail short of energy, reducing motility.

n.0: The penetrating enzymes sit in the acrosome on the head, which is normal here.
n.2: Fructose is supplied in seminal vesicle fluid; it is not stored in the sperm's midpiece.
n.3: The chromosomes are in the nucleus of the head, which is normal here.

q: After ovulation, the fimbriae sweep the secondary oocyte into the uterine tube. In a typical pregnancy, where does fertilization of the oocyte take place?
o: In the ampulla of the uterine tube
In the ruptured follicle of the ovary
In the functional layer of the endometrium
In the cervical canal of the uterus
w: Fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla, the wide outer portion of the uterine tube. Cilia and peristalsis then move the developing embryo to the uterus, where it implants in the endometrium.

n.1: The oocyte leaves the ovary at ovulation; the ruptured follicle then becomes the corpus luteum.
n.2: The endometrium is where the blastocyst implants about a week later, not where fertilization occurs.
n.3: Sperm pass through the cervix on the way up; fertilization happens farther along, in the uterine tube.

q: In a typical 28-day cycle, the dominant follicle releases a secondary oocyte around day 14. Which hormonal event directly causes this ovulation?
o: A sharp fall in estrogen from the follicles
A surge of FSH from the anterior pituitary
A surge of LH from the anterior pituitary
A surge of progesterone from the corpus luteum
w: High estrogen from the dominant (Graafian) follicle triggers the LH surge from the anterior pituitary, and the LH surge causes the follicle to rupture and release the secondary oocyte.

n.0: Estrogen is high, not falling, just before ovulation; high estrogen is what triggers the LH surge.
n.1: FSH stimulates follicle growth earlier in the follicular phase; the LH surge is what causes ovulation.
n.3: The corpus luteum forms from the ruptured follicle after ovulation, so its progesterone cannot trigger ovulation.

q: After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum. Which hormone does the corpus luteum mainly secrete, and what is its main effect on the uterus?
o: Progesterone, which keeps the endometrium in its secretory state
Estrogen, which rebuilds the endometrium after menstruation
FSH, which prepares the endometrium for implantation
Progesterone, which stimulates contractions of the myometrium
w: The corpus luteum secretes mainly progesterone (plus some estrogen). Progesterone maintains the thickened, secretory endometrium and relaxes the myometrium, preparing the uterus for implantation.

n.1: Rebuilding the endometrium in the proliferative phase is driven by estrogen from growing follicles before ovulation.
n.2: FSH is an anterior pituitary hormone that stimulates follicles; the corpus luteum does not secrete it.
n.3: Progesterone relaxes the myometrium; oxytocin is the hormone that stimulates uterine contractions.

q: A new mother notices that milk begins flowing from her breasts within seconds after her infant starts to suckle. Which hormone, from which gland, causes this milk ejection?
o: Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary
Prolactin from the anterior pituitary
Oxytocin from the anterior pituitary
Prolactin from the posterior pituitary
w: Oxytocin released from the posterior pituitary causes milk ejection (let-down). Prolactin from the anterior pituitary drives milk production.

n.1: Prolactin from the anterior pituitary stimulates milk production, not the rapid ejection of milk.
n.2: Oxytocin causes ejection, but it is released from the posterior pituitary, not the anterior pituitary.
n.3: Prolactin is an anterior pituitary hormone, and it governs milk production rather than ejection.

q: A home pregnancy test detects a hormone in urine shortly after a blastocyst implants. Which statement correctly identifies this hormone and its role in early pregnancy?
o: hCG from the mother's anterior pituitary, which keeps the corpus luteum alive
Progesterone from the corpus luteum, which keeps the endometrium intact
hCG from the embryo's trophoblast, which keeps the corpus luteum alive
LH from the mother's anterior pituitary, which triggers implantation
w: Pregnancy tests detect hCG, secreted by the trophoblast of the implanted blastocyst (later the placenta). hCG keeps the corpus luteum alive so it keeps secreting progesterone, which maintains the endometrium.

n.0: hCG is made by the embryo's trophoblast, not by the mother's pituitary.
n.1: Progesterone does maintain the endometrium, but home pregnancy tests detect hCG, not progesterone.
n.3: LH triggers ovulation, not implantation, and it is not the hormone pregnancy tests detect.

q: Which statement correctly describes the cell that the ovary releases at ovulation and the stage its meiosis has reached?
o: A mature ovum that completed meiosis II before leaving the ovary
A secondary oocyte that completes meiosis II if it is fertilized
A primary oocyte that completes meiosis I in the uterine tube
A secondary oocyte that completed meiosis II at the LH surge
w: Primary oocytes stay arrested in prophase I from before birth until puberty. Each cycle, one completes meiosis I just before ovulation, forming a secondary oocyte and the first polar body. The secondary oocyte is released and finishes meiosis II only if a sperm fertilizes it.

n.0: Meiosis II is not finished before ovulation; it is completed after fertilization.
n.2: Meiosis I is completed just before ovulation, so the released cell is already a secondary oocyte.
n.3: The LH surge is followed by completion of meiosis I, not meiosis II; meiosis II waits for fertilization.

q: Six primary oocytes and six primary spermatocytes complete meiosis normally, and each oocyte is fertilized so that meiosis II finishes. How many ova and how many sperm result in total?
o: 6 ova and 24 sperm
6 ova and 12 sperm
24 ova and 24 sperm
12 ova and 24 sperm
w: Two steps. (1) Oogenesis divides the cytoplasm unequally, so each primary oocyte yields 1 ovum plus polar bodies: 6 x 1 = 6 ova. (2) Spermatogenesis yields 4 sperm per primary spermatocyte: 6 x 4 = 24 sperm.

n.1: This counts 2 sperm per spermatocyte, which stops after meiosis I; meiosis II gives 4 per spermatocyte.
n.2: This treats oogenesis like spermatogenesis; polar bodies are not functional ova, so each oocyte gives 1 ovum.
n.3: This counts the first polar body as a second ovum; polar bodies degenerate and are not ova.

q: To slow preterm labor, a patient is given a drug that blocks oxytocin receptors in the uterus. The activity of which part of the uterus is this drug intended to reduce?
o: Myometrium, the smooth muscle layer
Cervix, the narrow lower neck
Endometrium, the glandular lining
Perimetrium, the outer serous layer
w: Two steps. (1) Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary stimulates uterine contractions in labor. (2) Those contractions come from the myometrium, the smooth muscle layer of the uterine wall. Blocking oxytocin receptors aims to quiet the myometrium.

n.1: The cervix is the lower neck that opens into the vagina; the contractions oxytocin drives come from the myometrium of the uterine wall.
n.2: The endometrium is the lining where implantation occurs and that is shed in menstruation; it does not generate labor contractions.
n.3: The perimetrium is the thin outer covering of the uterus; it does not produce the contractions of labor.

q: A 56-year-old woman has gone through menopause, and her ovaries no longer contain functioning follicles. Which pattern of hormone levels is expected in her blood?
o: High estrogen and progesterone with low FSH and LH
Low estrogen and progesterone with low FSH and LH
Low estrogen and progesterone with high FSH and LH
Low estrogen with high progesterone and low FSH
w: Two steps. (1) With the follicles exhausted, the ovaries make little estrogen and progesterone. (2) Those hormones normally exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so without them FSH and LH rise.

n.0: Without functioning follicles the ovaries cannot keep estrogen and progesterone high.
n.1: Falling ovarian hormones remove negative feedback, so FSH and LH rise rather than fall.
n.3: Progesterone comes mainly from the corpus luteum, which forms after ovulation, so it is low after menopause; FSH is high.

q: About a week after fertilization, the developing human implants in the endometrium of the uterus. Which stage implants, and how is it correctly described?
o: Blastocyst, a solid ball of cells made by cleavage
Morula, a hollow ball with a trophoblast layer
Blastocyst, a hollow ball with a trophoblast layer
Morula, a solid ball of cells made by cleavage
w: Development runs zygote, cleavage, morula, blastocyst, implantation, embryo (to week 8), fetus (week 9 to birth). The blastocyst implants about a week after fertilization, and its trophoblast later forms part of the placenta and secretes hCG.

n.0: Blastocyst is the right stage, but it is hollow (a fluid-filled cavity ringed by trophoblast); the solid ball made by cleavage is the morula.
n.1: A hollow ball with a trophoblast layer is the blastocyst; the morula is a solid ball with no cavity or trophoblast, and it comes first.
n.3: The morula is the solid ball formed by cleavage, but it develops into a blastocyst before implantation; the morula does not implant.

q: In the early embryo, which germ layer gives rise to the brain, spinal cord and the epidermis of the skin?
o: Trophoblast
Mesoderm
Endoderm
Ectoderm
w: The three germ layers: ectoderm forms the epidermis and the nervous system; mesoderm forms muscle, bone, blood, the heart and kidneys; endoderm forms the lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts, the liver and the pancreas.

n.0: The trophoblast is the outer layer of the blastocyst that helps form the placenta; it is not a germ layer of the embryo.
n.1: Mesoderm forms muscle, bone, blood, the heart and the kidneys, not the nervous system.
n.2: Endoderm forms the lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts, the liver and the pancreas.

q: Which pairing of an adult structure with the germ layer it develops from is correct?
o: Liver: ectoderm
Spinal cord: mesoderm
Epidermis: endoderm
Kidneys: mesoderm
w: Mesoderm forms muscle, bone, blood, the heart and the kidneys. Ectoderm forms the epidermis and nervous system, and endoderm forms the digestive and respiratory linings, liver and pancreas.

n.0: The liver develops from endoderm, along with the lining of the digestive tract.
n.1: The spinal cord is nervous tissue, which develops from ectoderm.
n.2: The epidermis comes from ectoderm; endoderm forms internal linings such as the gut lining.

q: Which vessel in the umbilical cord carries oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus?
o: The two umbilical veins
The single umbilical artery
The single umbilical vein
The two umbilical arteries
w: The umbilical cord normally holds one umbilical vein, which brings oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus, and two umbilical arteries, which carry deoxygenated blood and wastes back to the placenta.

n.0: A normal cord has only one umbilical vein, not two.
n.1: A normal cord has two umbilical arteries, and they carry deoxygenated blood, not oxygen-rich blood.
n.3: The two umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the fetus to the placenta.

q: Which statement correctly describes how materials pass between mother and fetus at the placenta?
o: Gases and nutrients cross; the two bloodstreams stay apart
Maternal and fetal blood mix, so gases equalize directly
Nutrients cross, but the fetus gets its O2 from amniotic fluid
Gases cross, but nutrients reach the fetus in amniotic fluid
w: At the placenta, oxygen, nutrients, wastes and some antibodies (IgG) diffuse between maternal and fetal blood across thin barriers. The two bloodstreams do not mix. The placenta also acts as an endocrine organ.

n.1: Maternal and fetal blood do not mix; exchange happens across the barrier between them.
n.2: Oxygen reaches the fetus from maternal blood across the placenta, not from the amniotic fluid.
n.3: Nutrients cross at the placenta into fetal blood; amniotic fluid cushions the fetus rather than feeding it.

q: At 6 weeks after fertilization, what is the developing human called, and what is the main process under way?
o: Fetus; organ systems are forming
Fetus; mainly growth and maturing
Embryo; organ systems are forming
Blastocyst; implanting in the uterus
w: The developing human is an embryo through week 8 after fertilization; this is when the organ systems form, so it is the period most sensitive to harmful agents. From week 9 to birth it is a fetus, and growth and maturation dominate.

n.0: The term fetus applies from week 9; at 6 weeks the developing human is still an embryo.
n.1: Growth and maturation describe the fetal period from week 9; at 6 weeks organs are still forming in the embryo.
n.3: The blastocyst implants about a week after fertilization, long before week 6.

q: During labor, stretching of the cervix triggers more oxytocin release, which strengthens contractions and stretches the cervix further. Which type of control is this, and which gland releases the oxytocin?
o: Positive feedback; anterior pituitary
Negative feedback; posterior pituitary
Positive feedback; posterior pituitary
Negative feedback; anterior pituitary
w: Each contraction increases cervical stretch, which increases oxytocin, which strengthens contractions: the response amplifies the stimulus, so it is positive feedback, ending with birth. Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.

n.0: This is positive feedback, but oxytocin is released from the posterior pituitary, not the anterior pituitary.
n.1: Negative feedback reverses a change; here the response amplifies the stretch until delivery, which is positive feedback.
n.3: Both parts are wrong: the loop amplifies the change, and oxytocin comes from the posterior pituitary.

q: Which statement correctly describes dizygotic (fraternal) twins?
o: Two zygotes form; the twins are as alike as ordinary siblings
Two zygotes form; the twins carry identical sets of genes
One zygote splits; the twins carry identical sets of genes
One zygote splits; the twins are as alike as ordinary siblings
w: Dizygotic twins form when two oocytes are fertilized by two different sperm, giving two zygotes; genetically they are as alike as any siblings. Monozygotic (identical) twins form when one zygote splits, so they share the same genes.

n.1: Two separate zygotes come from two oocytes and two sperm, so their genes differ like those of ordinary siblings.
n.2: This describes monozygotic (identical) twins, not dizygotic twins.
n.3: A single zygote that splits gives monozygotic twins, and those twins share identical genes.
